entries.title: Direct tax and apportionment
entries.summary: The Constitution requires certain direct federal taxes to be apportioned by population among states, subject to the Sixteenth Amendment for income taxes.
entries.details: Murphy II discusses Article I and distinguishes taxes on property ownership from taxes on transactions or activities.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 85

entries.title: Article I taxing power and constitutional limits
entries.summary: Congress has broad Article I power to lay taxes; direct taxes require apportionment except to the extent the Sixteenth Amendment permits unapportioned income taxes.
entries.details: The reproduced Murphy II excerpt reasons that taxing its award can be an excise on a transaction, satisfying the constitutional framework.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 85

entries.title: Perez v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. The payments were taxable compensation, not excludable damages for personal physical injury.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Perez v. Commissioner, 144 T.C. 51 (2015), reproduced pp. 90–94
entries.facts: Perez underwent painful injections and egg retrieval procedures under contracts that paid her $20,000 for compliance with the procedure. The contracts disclaimed payment for eggs and allocated medical risks to Perez.
entries.issue: Does contractual compensation for undergoing a voluntary painful medical procedure count as excludable damages on account of personal physical injuries under §104(a)(2)?
entries.holding: No. The payments were taxable compensation, not excludable damages for personal physical injury.
entries.reasoning: Perez voluntarily agreed to the procedures in exchange for compensation; the clinic did not pay damages for a wrong or compensable injury. The regulation's removal of the formal tort-rights requirement did not turn voluntary contractual services payments into damages.
entries.rule: §104(a)(2) requires qualifying damages on account of personal physical injury/sickness; compensation under a bargained-for voluntary services contract is not automatically damages.
entries.exam: Distinguish contract compensation for voluntarily undergone procedures from a recovery for a legally compensable physical injury.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish contract compensation for voluntarily undergone procedures from a recovery for a legally compensable physical injury.

entries.title: Structured settlement
entries.summary: A legal settlement that pays qualified damages over time rather than as a single lump sum.
entries.details: The textbook explains that qualifying periodic payments for physical injuries may receive special tax treatment, creating a timing advantage.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 94

entries.title: Periodic payments for personal physical injury
entries.summary: Under §104(a)(2), qualifying physical-injury damages may be excludable whether paid in a lump sum or periodic payments.
entries.details: Structured settlements require careful analysis of entitlement and economic control; the reading highlights favorable treatment of certain deferred-payment components.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 94

entries.title: Policy rationale for physical injury exclusion
entries.summary: Compensation arguably restores lost physical well-being rather than creating a net economic gain.
entries.details: The text contrasts physical with emotional/reputational injuries and asks why nominally similar compensation can be taxed differently.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79

topics.title: F. Illegal Income
topics.description: Taxability of unlawful gains, claims of right and restitution.

entries.title: Illegal proceeds may be taxable gross income
entries.summary: Unlawful gains can constitute gross income under §61, even if the recipient may later be required to repay them.
entries.details: James v. United States is referenced for the general principle: receipt without consensual recognition of an obligation to repay and without restriction can be taxable.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 96
entries.examTrap: Illegal character of income does not remove it from §61.

entries.title: Claim of right
entries.summary: A taxpayer's practical dominion over funds, without an acknowledged limitation or consensual obligation to repay, may support current inclusion.
entries.details: The source compares typical embezzlement proceeds against loans or prompt secured repayment arrangements.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 97

entries.title: Obligation to repay
entries.summary: A recognized duty to return money, relevant to whether receipt is a taxable accession to wealth or nonincome borrowing.
entries.details: Do not mistake a purely subjective intention to repay for a legally and factually supported borrowing obligation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 97

entries.title: Gilbert v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Second Circuit reversed the Tax Court; under its unusual facts, the withdrawals were not income when acquired.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 96
entries.facts: Gilbert, a corporation president and principal shareholder, withdrew nearly $1.96 million in company funds without advance authorization to meet stock-purchase margin calls. Shortly afterward, he gave demand promissory notes and secured them with assets exceeding the debt's value; the corporate board accepted the security but did not ratify his initial actions.
entries.issue: Were Gilbert's unauthorized withdrawals taxable embezzlement income when he intended and secured prompt repayment?
entries.holding: The Second Circuit reversed the Tax Court; under its unusual facts, the withdrawals were not income when acquired.
entries.reasoning: Unlike typical embezzlement, Gilbert recognized repayment obligations, reasonably expected to repay, believed the withdrawals would be approved, and promptly delivered adequate collateral. These facts distinguished James and Buff.
entries.rule: Carefully compare initial intent, recognized debt, prompt security, reasonable repayment ability, and corporation's response. Do not treat a general post hoc promise to repay as enough.

exam.source: Gilbert v. Commissioner, 552 F.2d 478 (2d Cir. 1977), reproduced pp. 96–98

examApplication.source: Gilbert v. Commissioner, 552 F.2d 478 (2d Cir. 1977), reproduced pp. 96–98

entries.title: James v. United States (supporting citation)
entries.summary: The textbook cites James for the general taxability of embezzled funds.
entries.details: James is referenced within Gilbert; it is not a separately reproduced assigned opinion in the supplied pages.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 97

topics.title: G. Gain on Sale of a Home
topics.description: Section 121 home-sale gain exclusion and limitations.

entries.title: IRC §121 — Principal residence exclusion
entries.summary: A qualifying taxpayer may exclude up to $250,000 of gain on sale of a principal residence, or generally $500,000 for qualifying joint filers.
entries.details: General rule: taxpayer owned and used the property as principal residence for at least two years during the five-year period ending at sale; subject to frequency, filing and other conditions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 100
entries.elements: Ownership and principal residence use: generally 2 of the 5 years before sale. Standard cap: $250,000; qualifying MFJ cap: $500,000.
entries.examTrap: A vacation property does not qualify merely because it is owned for two years; the principal-residence use requirement matters.

entries.title: IRC §121 — Joint-return conditions
entries.summary: A $500,000 exclusion for qualifying married joint filers generally requires meeting joint-return, use, ownership and other statutory requirements.
entries.details: The reading notes that both spouses must satisfy the use test, while the ownership condition can be satisfied under the statutory joint-filer rules.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 101

entries.title: IRC §121 — Once-every-two-years limit
entries.summary: A taxpayer generally cannot claim the full §121 exclusion if it was used on a different sale within the preceding two years.
entries.details: The reading discusses reduced exclusions when sales arise from qualifying changes in employment, health, or certain unforeseen circumstances.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 101

entries.title: Principal residence
entries.summary: The home that serves as the taxpayer's main residence for purposes of §121's use requirement.
entries.details: This characterization is factual and distinct from owning a secondary home or investment property.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 100

entries.title: Taxable gain after §121 exclusion
entries.summary: Taxable gain = max(0, realized home-sale gain − allowable §121 exclusion).
entries.details: Textbook example: single taxpayer's $100,000-basis residence sold for $400,000; realized gain $300,000, $250,000 excluded, $50,000 taxable (assuming full eligibility).
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 101
entries.examApplication: Compute realized gain first, then determine §121 eligibility and exclusion limit.

entries.title: Pre-1997 home-sale gain rules
entries.summary: Former §1034 allowed rollover-style gain deferral on reinvestment in another home; prior §121 had a one-time older-taxpayer exclusion.
entries.details: These rules are repealed and appear in the reading only to explain the current §121 regime.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 102

legalWarning.label: REPEALED PRE-1997 LAW
legalWarning.reason: The old §1034 rollover provision and previous one-time home-sale exclusion were superseded by the 1997 enactment of current §121.
